newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Actor James Garner still plays the maverick.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Actor James Garner still plays the maverick.

text.p: Don't tell James Garner he's getting too old to play sexy, leading man roles.
At age 68, Garner still has his rugged good looks and rakish charm, and his wry sense of humour hasn't softened in the least.
Garner's latest movie part, as philandering ex-president Matthew Douglas in "My Fellow Americans," fits his image. The film opened nationally last week.
"I like the fact he is a womanizer, and protocol is not his thing. That's the way I am." Garner says about the Douglas character. "I'm not a womanizer, but I don't like protocol."
In the 1950s when TV Westerns were filled with hardened cowboys, along came Garner's smooth-talking gambler, Bret Maverick, in the hit show "Maverick".

Television private eyes were all business during the 1970s, but Garner's Jim Rockford added some laughs to the genre. And his 1980s legal tussle over royalties from "The Rockford Files" boosted his image in Hollywood as an independent thinker.

He is still an individualist. Wearing a black sweater and black trousers that highlight his dark hair, Garner is sitting in a Beverly Hills hotel room with his feet propped up on the table, spouting off about his 40 years in show business, stardom and politics.
He hates politicians. "You can't trust 'em," he says in a matter-of-fact tone, not unlike the way ex-president Douglas might say it in "My Fellow Americans."

A scandal is about to rock the foundation of the White House in this comedy that puts a human face on presidents. Implicated in the wrongdoing are the Democrat Douglas and his arch-rival Republican Russell Kramer, played by Jack Lemmon.
CONTRASTING PRESIDENTS
Kramer is a married man who feigns concern about the children of America when he's really more interested in how much money he makes on product endorsements.

Douglas, by contrast, is in the throes of a divorce because he can't keep his hands off other women, and he speaks his mind about other politicians -- especially Kramer -- with little regard to how it will appear in the media.
Through a number of coincidences, the two are thrown together on a road trip across the midwestern United States in an attempt to clear their names.
And their journey takes a few wild turns. "There's at least 20 to 25 good belly laughs throughout," Garner says with a smile.
When asked about the state of Hollywood, Garner doesn't mince words. "Today you've got lawyers and people who have no creative sense of making pictures. Making the deal is the big thing."

He believes the best movies are made by independent filmmakers because studios are too concerned about special effects and action, and he says the best writing is in stories told on cable television because cable networks can tackle issues that truly affect people.
NO RETIREMENT

Though he's caustic about the industry, he's not about to retire. He says he is committed to doing another "Rockford Files" special, and he is even talking about working on a half-hour situation comedy.

He credits his longevity to a strong desire to avoid superstardom. "I never wanted to be number one at the box office because I had nowhere to go but down," he says about being a top draw since starring with Doris Day in a string of movies in the 1960s. "I never wanted to be a star. I just wanted to work."
Garner thinks today's crop of young actors achieve their celebrity too easily without sweat and hard work. "They have no strength of character."
